reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: General
sections.body: Drilled shaft behavior is highly dependent on local geology and construction procedure details, making accurate performance prediction from standardized methods difficult. Site-specific load tests performed under realistic conditions improve accuracy and reliability. Because load tests reduce prediction variability, larger resistance factors are justified when tests are performed. Two general purposes: (1) load transfer tests — obtain detailed information on side and base resistance distribution to allow improved design; best performed on test shafts constructed in advance of production installation; (2) proof tests — verify that test shaft can sustain a given load, thus verifying strength/serviceability requirements. Benefits of load testing: direct measure of resistance in project-specific geology and with project construction methods; improved reliability allows higher resistance factors; potential reduction in shaft length or rock excavation. Limitations: limited benefit in highly variable geology from single test; substantial time and money investment; may not recover cost for projects with few shafts; design may not be controlled by geotechnical strength (e.g., scour or lateral loading governs).
key_points: Load transfer test: detailed side/base resistance distribution for improved design
Proof test: verify shaft can sustain required load — strength/serviceability verification
Load tests justify larger resistance factors — directly reduces uncertainty
Preferred: load tests on non-production test shafts in advance of production installation
Minimum recommendation: number of load tests ≥2% of total production drilled shafts

sections.title: Load Test Timing Options
sections.body: Design-phase tests: greatest benefit — results can be incorporated to optimize design and constructability; comparative testing of alternatives (drilled shafts vs. driven piles); reduces constructability risks for bidders; allows construction to proceed immediately to production; requires separate contract with drawings, specifications, permits. Start of construction tests: design benefits from higher resistance factors; incorporated into project contract; can include adjustments to shaft tip elevation; limited opportunity for major design changes; contractor must bid on worst-case conditions. Proof tests on production shafts: quality assurance and verification; minimal schedule impact; no separate contract; test on questionable shaft possible; AASHTO lacks established procedure/resistance factors for proof tests; unfavorable result requires expensive remediation. Multiple test locations required for large sites: when geologic character differs; when average calibrated resistance varies by factor of 2 or more from test location; when location is far from test shaft; for large number of shafts (≥2% load tests of total production shafts).
key_points: Design-phase: greatest benefit; requires separate contract; best for schedule optimization
Start of construction: most common; incorporated in project contract; limited design flexibility
Proof tests on production shafts: QA only; AASHTO lacks established resistance factors for proof tests
Multiple tests: needed when geologic character differs or calibrated resistance varies 2× or more

sections.title: Load Tests to Measure Axial Resistance
sections.body: Planning objectives: identify most critical resistance components (base vs. side; specific stratum); assess effect of construction method (slurry type, exposure time, base cleanliness, grouting); measure load-displacement relationships; verify design assumptions. Test shaft location: match geology of production shafts; consider number needed for variable sites. Test shaft construction: match production shaft diameter, length, construction method, and installation procedures as closely as possible. Test methods: (1) conventional top-loading with kentledge (dead weight) or reaction frame — practical for lower capacity shafts; very large loads impractical for high capacity shafts; (2) bi-directional load cell (O-cell) — hydraulic jack embedded in shaft; loads shaft upward and downward simultaneously; can test very high capacity shafts economically; Osterberg cell and similar devices; converts separate upward and downward test results to equivalent top-load curve; ASTM D8169/D8169M; most common method for high-capacity drilled shafts; (3) rapid compression force pulse (Statnamic) — combustion gas or drop mass applies compressive force pulse at top; ASTM D7383 Procedure A (gas) or B (drop mass); (4) high strain dynamic testing — drop weight delivers blow to top of shaft; ASTM D4945; signal matching analysis. Instrumentation: vibrating wire or resistive strain gauges on reinforcing bars at multiple elevations to determine load distribution between strata and between side and base resistance; telltales (rods) measure displacement at tip and selected elevations; accelerometers and force transducers for dynamic tests. Interpretation: strain gauge data used to construct load-transfer curves; equivalent top-load vs. displacement from O-cell test; Davisson criterion or other method for failure load from conventional test.
key_points: Bi-directional (O-cell) method: most common for high-capacity drilled shafts; ASTM D8169/D8169M
Rapid compression force pulse (Statnamic): ASTM D7383; applicable for medium-high capacity shafts
High-strain dynamic testing: ASTM D4945; requires signal matching analysis
Instrumentation: strain gauges at multiple elevations to separate side and base resistance
O-cell converts upward/downward test results to equivalent top-load displacement curve
Load test justifies resistance factors up to φ = 0.65-0.75 vs. φ = 0.50-0.55 without testing

sections.title: Load Tests to Measure Lateral Resistance
sections.body: Lateral load tests directly measure load-displacement response under lateral and moment loading. Most often performed as conventional lateral load test at top of shaft using a hydraulic jack reacting against an adjacent shaft or a reaction wall. Test measures lateral deflection and rotation at top. Instrumented shafts include inclinometers or slope indicators for deflection profile vs. depth; strain gauges for moment distribution. Results used to calibrate p-y curves for the site-specific soil conditions. Bi-directional lateral tests possible but less common. Important distinction: lateral tests to large displacements (>1/2 in.) can produce non-reversible structural damage to production shafts — lateral tests generally should be performed on test shafts rather than production shafts. Seismic load testing considerations: cyclic lateral load tests can simulate earthquake loading effects on p-y curves; cyclic softening of cohesive soils affects lateral resistance.
key_points: Lateral test: hydraulic jack between test shaft and reaction shaft/wall; measure force and deflection
Inclinometers provide deflection profile vs. depth; strain gauges provide moment profile
Results calibrate p-y curves for site-specific conditions
Large lateral displacements (>1/2 in.) can damage production shafts — test on test shafts only
Cyclic lateral tests simulate seismic loading effects

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter described field load testing methods, planning considerations, and interpretation for axial and lateral loading. Load tests reduce uncertainty and justify higher resistance factors in design. Bi-directional (O-cell) testing is the most practical and economical method for high-capacity drilled shafts. Design-phase testing provides the greatest benefit; proof testing on production shafts provides minimum quality assurance. Instrumentation is essential to maximize information from test programs.
